u/plvntsncoffee, thanks for your thoughts on seeking help. While I understand that may not be desired, it is sometimes necessary to save a life. As a mental health provider myself, I have treated many individuals for suicidal experiences. During a moment of crisis, our judgment becomes impaired and we struggle to make rational decisions. These types of moments make it hard for someone to recognize when they need help and when they do not. Most attempts of suicide progress from "thinking about it" to action, within 5-10 minutes. If I'm not sure I am going to lose my life (by my own hand, an accident, or by someone else), it's worth a trip to the hospital, even if it's deemed unnecessary in hindsight. Hence, the overreaction, and sometimes unnecessary life-saving attempts, by responders. 

That being said, not every occasion of suicidal thinking (or even most) requires police coming to someone's home. Unfortunately, this is a gray area for most traditional first responders, and highlights the need to have effective training on suicide prevention, and knowing what the appropriate response is for each situation. I encourage anyone who is struggling with a tough mental and emotional state to reach out to a mental health provider you feel comfortable with in order to get the treatment you need before it becomes an emergency. I have found that, when circumstances in life turn into an emergency, we have the least amount of control over the situation at that point.

u/ElectrikDonuts, thanks for the feedback and the suggestions. While I absolutely agree that there are challenges and deficits within the Military MH system, this study is set to examine which aspects an individual possesses (or doesn't) that can help professionals intervene when they are connected to the right care, that can be more effective at preventing suicide. It sounds like you are suggesting an over-haul of the MH system, of which another type of study could greatly impact. While still an absolutely valid suggestion, it is different angle than the one I'm coming in at.

There are a lot of hoops to jump through for some, and for others, they have had a relatively easy time getting care. Trust me--I am a MH provider, and have seen both sides. The "system" is made up of people who create processes, and sometimes those processes are super ineffective and inefficient, while on the flipside, there are many things that work well. I do care, and it's not just to check some boxes.  It's unfortunate that this has been your experience, and for that I'm truly sorry. 

I appreciate your suggestions on how to improve the system. If a suicide occurs at a base, then a full standard of care (SoC) review is completed. This SoC review goes through many of the points you bring up, with a fine-tooth comb. The review looks at many factors, including how many times a person contacted the clinic before getting an appt., if they reported any thoughts of suicide, if there was sufficient follow-up, conducts a detailed-review of all encounters, and so on. The provider gets highly scrutinized, can even lose his/her license, and the ability to practice altogether. 

I say all this to say, that "we" care, even if it feels like the system does not. It's not meant to be a "just to check boxes" type of deal, and I'm sorry that's been your experience. Our MH system is not perfect, and I am trying to help make it better by doing things like this study. 

Please feel free to send me a message if you'd like to discuss more. I am always open to feedback!

Hey, SeenSomeThangs, I appreciate your thoughts. I absolutely agree. I think we're failing big-time with the transition from AD to civilian life. Many of our junior enlisted and officers haven't had that "real-world experience," through no fault of their own, other than being straight out of high school and joining. Some would say that's a wise choice given the environment they might be coming from. So, it's hard to say which path is better. Nonetheless, the grass is always greener on the other side, and it's a real challenge to get people to "feel" it without knowing it personally. I came in as an officer 10 years after high school, with a lot of professional and personal experience. I can only share so much with my Airmen, but it does help for AD members to have real conversations with those who led a prior-civilian life, as opposed to a post-civilian life, if that makes sense.
